why: A room is needed for every meeting that is running at the same moment, so the answer is the maximum number of intervals overlapping at any point: a classic intervals sweep (or a min-heap of end times).
hints: Think about the busiest moment of the day. How many meetings are running then, and could you ever get away with fewer rooms than that?
The answer is the maximum overlap. Sort starts and ends separately and sweep: a start opens a room, an end frees one. Equivalently, sort by start and keep a min-heap of end times of rooms in use.
Heap version: sort by start; for each meeting pop the heap top if it ended at or before this start, then push this end. Answer = max heap size. O(n log n).
pitfalls: A meeting ending at time t frees its room for a meeting starting at t: [1,5] and [5,8] need only one room. Process ends before starts at equal times.
Sorting intervals by end instead of start breaks the heap approach.
statement:
You are given a list of meetings, intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]. A meeting occupies a room from start_i up to (but not including) end_i, so a meeting that ends at time t and another that starts at t can share a room. Return the minimum number of conference rooms needed so that every meeting has a room.

Worked example. intervals = [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]].

  • At time 5, meetings [0,30] and [5,10] are both running: 2 rooms in use.
  • At time 10 the [5,10] meeting ends and frees its room.
  • At time 15, [15,20] reuses that freed room while [0,30] keeps the other.

Never more than 2 meetings overlap, so the answer is 2.
